mu-3e7418f2.stem: Which muscle, although in the forearm and supplied by the radial nerve, flexes the elbow in the mid-prone position?
mu-3e7418f2.explanation: Brachioradialis is a muscle of the extensor (posterior) compartment and is supplied by the radial nerve; but because it passes in front of the elbow joint it flexes the elbow, especially with the forearm in the mid-position.

mu-f40cfc25.stem: Which of the following does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
mu-f40cfc25.explanation: Nine tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) pass through the carpal tunnel with the median nerve. The palmaris longus tendon passes in front of the flexor retinaculum to join the palmar aponeurosis; it is absent in about 15% of people and is used as a tendon graft.

mu-843fc5bd.stem: After a radial head fracture the patient cannot extend the fingers at the MCP joints. He can lift the wrist, but it deviates radially. There is no sensory loss in the hand. Which nerve is injured?
options: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Main trunk of the radial nerve (in the radial groove)
Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve)
mu-843fc5bd.explanation: The deep branch passes through supinator (arcade of Frohse) to become the posterior interosseous nerve and supplies the finger extensors and ECU. ECRL is spared because its branch arises before the division; wrist extension deviates radially. As the sensory superficial branch is unaffected, there is no sensory loss.

mu-7e2f1848.stem: A 40-year-old tennis player has tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and pain on resisted wrist extension. The origin tendon of which muscle is most often affected?
mu-7e2f1848.explanation: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) is an overuse degeneration of the common extensor origin, most often the ECRB tendon. Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) involves the common flexor–pronator origin.

mu-49e4b965.stem: Which tendon forms the ulnar (medial) border of the anatomical snuffbox?
mu-49e4b965.explanation: The radial border of the snuffbox is formed by the APL and EPB tendons, the ulnar border by the EPL tendon. Its floor contains the scaphoid and trapezium, and the radial artery runs within it. The EPL tendon changes direction around the dorsal tubercle of the radius (Lister's).

mu-ffeff985.stem: A new mother complains of pain on the radial side of the wrist when holding her baby. Pain increases when the thumb is held in the palm and the wrist is deviated ulnarly (Finkelstein test). Which tendons are affected?
options: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Extensor digitorum and extensor digiti minimi
Flexor pollicis longus and flexor carpi radialis
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
mu-ffeff985.explanation: De Quervain's tenosynovitis is inflammation of the sheath of the APL and EPB tendons, which run together in the first dorsal compartment over the radial styloid.

mu-da0f7eac.stem: What are the nerve supply and action of flexor carpi ulnaris?
options: Median nerve – pronation of the forearm
Median nerve – flexion and abduction of the wrist
Ulnar nerve – flexion and adduction (ulnar deviation) of the wrist
Radial nerve – adduction of the wrist
Ulnar nerve – extension of the wrist
mu-da0f7eac.explanation: FCU is the only superficial forearm flexor supplied by the ulnar nerve; it attaches through the pisiform to the hamate and 5th metacarpal. FCR is supplied by the median nerve and deviates the wrist radially.

mu-3d11398e.stem: Which thumb muscle is supplied by the ulnar nerve?
options: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
mu-3d11398e.explanation: The thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, superficial head of FPB) are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Adductor pollicis and the deep head of FPB receive the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

mu-2e66f083.stem: What is the action of the lumbricals in the hand?
options: To flex only the distal phalanges
To flex the MCP joints and extend the interphalangeal joints
To extend the MCP joints and flex the interphalangeal joints
mu-2e66f083.explanation: The lumbricals arise from the FDP tendons and attach to the radial side of the extensor hood. They therefore flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints (the writing position). The 1st and 2nd lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve, the 3rd and 4th by the ulnar nerve.

mu-e4b2117a.stem: The patient is asked to grip a sheet of paper firmly between thumb and index finger; when the paper is pulled he tries to hold it by flexing the tip joint of the thumb (Froment's sign). Which muscle is weak and which nerve is damaged?
options: Flexor pollicis longus – anterior interosseous nerve
mu-e4b2117a.explanation: When adductor pollicis is weak the patient uses FPL, supplied by the median nerve, to hold the paper, and the IP joint of the thumb flexes. This is a classic sign of ulnar nerve damage.

mu-f344fd2c.stem: In carpal tunnel syndrome, why is sensation over the lateral half of the palm usually preserved?
options: The palm is supplied by the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
The palmar skin is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
The palmar skin is supplied only by the ulnar nerve.
The palmar branch of the median nerve arises before the carpal tunnel and passes in front of the retinaculum.
mu-f344fd2c.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch arises a few centimetres above the wrist and does not use the tunnel. So in carpal tunnel syndrome sensory loss is limited to the fingers (palmar surface of the lateral 3½ digits); if the palm is involved, the lesion is more proximal.

mu-2897d8ef.stem: Which statement about the palmar and dorsal interossei is true?
options: They are all supplied by the median nerve.
The palmar interossei adduct the fingers, the dorsal interossei abduct them.
The dorsal interossei adduct the fingers.
The axis is the 4th finger, that of the middle finger.
mu-2897d8ef.explanation: 'PAD–DAB': Palmar ADduct, Dorsal ABduct. Movements are defined relative to the axis of the middle finger. All the interossei are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; like the lumbricals they flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints.

mu-123724d0.stem: Why is the claw-hand deformity milder in a patient whose ulnar nerve is injured at the elbow than in one injured at the wrist?
options: At the elbow all the lumbricals are spared.
At the elbow the ulnar part of FDP is also paralysed, so IP flexion of the 4th–5th fingers is reduced.
At the elbow the interossei are spared.
At the wrist the median nerve is also affected.
At the wrist the extensors are paralysed.
mu-123724d0.explanation: In a claw hand the MCP joints are hyperextended and the IP joints flexed; the flexion is produced by FDP. In a high (elbow) lesion the ulnar half of FDP is also paralysed, so clawing is less. This is known as the 'ulnar paradox'.

mu-1b433a0a.stem: After hip surgery the patient can walk on level ground but has difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. Which muscle and nerve are affected?
mu-1b433a0a.explanation: Gluteus maximus is the powerful extensor of the hip and comes into play especially when moving from flexion to extension (rising from a chair, climbing stairs, running). Its contribution to normal walking is small.
